extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, judges, and legal practitioners handling patent interferences
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding legal principles and procedural rules governing priority (first inventor), reduction to practice, caveats, abandonment/public-use bars, competency and transmission of evidence in patent interference and application contests under the 1836/1839 acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: No statutory requirement to reduce to practice before patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no law which requires an inventor to put his invention in practice or use, before obtaining his patent; it is perfectly immaterial whether the subsequent inventor had put it in practice or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant need not have brought the invention into actual public use to be entitled to a patent; filing the specification/drawings/model as required by statute can suffice (see later 'reduced to practice' explanation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-user does not forfeit rights absent abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: A citizen patentee cannot lose his right by non user, unless it amount to evidence of an abandonment of the patent; the question of an abandonment of a patent is a question for the jury on a trial at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay or mere non-use alone is insufficient to forfeit rights; abandonment is a fact question for a jury and must be proved as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public communication can give priority when prior inventor kept secret (Dolland doctrine), but exceptions exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Where one inventor confines his invention to his closet and does not communicate it to the public, and a subsequent inventor obtains a patent and brings it into use, the patentee is to be considered the first inventor. But this doctrine does not justify defeating a bona fide prior inventor who is using reasonable diligence in adapting and perfecting his invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority via public disclosure applies primarily to simultaneous independent discoveries where prior inventor made no public disclosure or steps toward patenting; if prior inventor was diligently preparing to apply or perfecting, courts will protect his claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'reduced to practice'
rubrics_metrics.description: "Reduced to practice" generally means the reducing it into such form that it may be used, so as not to be a mere theory; if a machine is described so that it may be made and used, and especially if a model is made, the invention may be said to be reduced to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a specification and furnishing drawings and a model (where the case admits) can constitute reduction to practice for purposes of priority; the actual size of a model is immaterial if it demonstrates practicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect (and limits) of entering a caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: The caveat does not create any right; it is simply a request to be favored with information. It gives no notice to the world or to the interfering applicant; it is notice to the Commissioner only and is locked up in the secret and confidential archives of the office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entering a caveat is for the inventor's convenience to alert the Commissioner, but omission of a caveat neither strengthens nor impairs title in the eyes of the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay in applying not barred by statute; abandonment is the decisive issue
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute does not limit any time in which the inventor must apply for a patent; delay is unimportant unless it amounts to evidence of abandonment of the claim. If there be any limit of the time of application, it must be a reasonable limit, and that is proper matter for the consideration of a jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commissioner should not refuse patents for mere delay absent statutory grounds; issues of intent and abandonment are typically for a jury and determined under reasonable-time standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1 — Written, verified statements setting forth points at issue
rubrics_metrics.description: All statements, declarations, evidence, &c., shall be in writing, setting forth, minutely and particularly, the point or points at issue, and shall be verified by oath or affirmation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initiatory proceedings and uncontested applications are expected to conform to this rule; ensures clarity and verifiability of the matters submitted to the office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 2 — File all statements, proofs and evidence before hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: All statements, declarations, proofs, and evidence, shall be filed in the Patent Office, by the parties respectively, before the day of hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties to a contested case must file their evidence in advance so the Commissioner and opposing parties have fair access prior to the hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 3 — Notice and opportunity for cross-examination for depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the deposition of a witness or witnesses be taken by either party, notice should be given to the opposite party of the time and place when and where such deposition or depositions will be taken; so that the opposite party ... shall have full opportunity to cross-examine the witness or witnesses. Such notice shall, with proof of service, be attached to the deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short notice or failure to afford opportunity to cross-examine may be objectionable; if a party nevertheless appears and cross-examines, the lateness may be excused though it might justify a request for more time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 4 — No evidence at hearing unless taken and filed according to rules (subject to narrow exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: No evidence, statement, or declaration, touching the matter at issue, will be considered upon the said day of hearing, which shall not have been taken and filed in compliance with these rules: Provided, that if either party shall be unable, from good and sufficient reasons, to procure the testimony ... it shall be the duty of said party to give notice of the same to the Commissioner ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule binds the Commissioner as an assurance he will not consider untimely evidence; exceptions exist for good cause with notice to the Commissioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 5 — All evidence shall be sealed, addressed, and certified by the magistrate
rubrics_metrics.description: All evidence, &c., shall be sealed up and addressed to the Commissioner of Patents, by the persons before whom it shall be taken, and so certified thereon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The certification (including that the deposition was sealed by the magistrate) is a material formality and a security against alteration; omission of the required certification is sufficient ground for excluding the deposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest of witness may render testimony incompetent
rubrics_metrics.description: It is one of the rules in law, that no man can be a witness in his own cause, unless made competent by statute, or by being called upon by the opposing party ... If the witness is interested he is excluded, however small the amount of interest may be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interest even of small degree can impair competency; where interest exists but is common to all claimants or uncertain, the weight rather than admissibility may be affected (credibility considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner bound by his promulgated rules and cannot retroactively dispense with them
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules, made in conformity with the law, while they remain unabrogated, are as binding as the law itself. In the rules which the Commissioner has promulgated, he has not reserved any right to dispense with them, in particular cases, at his pleasure. After a deposition has been taken while the rules were in force, his dispensation cannot affect that deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once rules are in force, parties acquire rights under them; the Commissioner may not ignore or waive those rules retroactively in contested cases where parties relied on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use with consent for more than two years prior to application bars patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of the machine, with his consent, for two years prior to his application is a bar to his claim; the defendant might defend himself under the 15th section of the act of 1836, and the 7th section of the act of 1839, by showing that the machine had been in public use, with the consent of the patentee, for more than two years prior to the application for the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention was in public use with the inventor's consent for the statutory pre-application period, that may constitute an absolute statutory bar to patentability/enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint invention test — contribution to principle and reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention consisted both of the discovery of the principle and the reduction of it to practice. The man who reduces to practice the theory of another who assists in the reduction of it to practice cannot be considered as the sole inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of sole vs joint inventorship depends on who discovered the principle (the underlying idea) and who contributed to its reduction to practice; those who suggested the principle may be joint inventors even if another constructed the machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy when Commissioner refuses patents — bill in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: In all cases where patents are refused, for any reason whatever, either by the Commissioner of Patents, or by the chief justice of the District of Columbia, upon appeals from the decision of said Commissioner, the applicant may have remedy by bill in equity ... and the court ... may adjudge that such applicant is entitled ... to have and receive a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant denied by the Commissioner has an available equitable remedy; a favorable adjudication authorizes the Commissioner to issue a patent upon compliance with requisitions.
